title.narrative: Improving experiences of severe stigmatising skin diseases in Ghana and Ethiopia

description.narrative: Objectives: 1. Evaluate integrated strategies for early diagnosis, adherence support and stigma reduction to improve outcomes for individuals with SSSDs 2. Undertake a multi-centre RCT of Dialkylcarbamoyl chloride (DACC)-coated dressings to improve wound healing in BU 3. To promote collaboration and build research capacity in Ghana and Ethiopia.

The Skin Health Africa Research Programme (SHARP) aims to improve outcomes for people with severe stigmatising skin diseases (SSSDs) in Ghana and Ethiopia by strengthening the care cascade through scalable strategies for earlier detection, improving management to reduce disability and counteracting stigma and discrimination. SHARP is a collaboration between the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) in the UK, the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research, University of Ghana (NMIMR UG) and the Kumasi Centre for Collaborative Research in Tropical Medicine of Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KCCR, KNUST) in Ghana, and the Armauer Hansen Research Institute (AHRI) and Addis Ababa University (AAU) in Ethiopia.
Towards achieving objective 1, an initial formative work was done in the Atwima Mponua District in the Ashanti Region Ghana. We conducted a mixed-methods study employing several data collection activities. First, we exhaustively assessed all public health facilities in the district, conducting a Service Availability and Readiness Assessment at 16 facilities and reviewing records from all 9 health centres and the Atwima Mponua district hospital. Qualitative data were gathered through purposively sampled interviews and discussions: 33 health workers, 8 affected individuals, 6 household caregivers, and 3 community members involved in care were interviewed, with participants for the latter groups identified via snowball sampling. Additionally, 7 Focus Group Discussions and 8 interviews with regional and national key informants were held. Community engagement included 14 purposively selected community meetings. Finally, a purposive review of 6 key national and international policy documents relevant to skin NTDs was completed. The interventions involved a combination of facility-based, community-based, and patient-centred activities. First, the Decentralised Care Model focused on strengthening health facility capacity. This included establishing and implementing wound management protocols, rolling out clinical training with job aids, and ensuring the provision of diagnostics, wound care packs, and treatments to health centres and CHPS compounds. Information systems were strengthened through patient tracking and supply chain monitoring, while wound care clinics were strengthened and supported through regular supervision by district disease control officers. Second, the Self-Care Delivery Pathway enabled less severe cases to be managed at home. Health workers were trained to identify clinically suitable patients using an assessment algorithm. Those eligible received condition-specific self-care plan booklets and basic management kits, and were regularly reviewed to ensure proper follow-up. Third, Community Engagement and Referral activities aimed to raise awareness and promote case-finding. This involved delivering mass education events in schools and community centres using presentations. Non-Ghana Health Service actors such as school health staff and community volunteers were engaged to refer suspected cases to health facilities, thereby widening the referral network and integrating community-based detection with formal care. Together, these activities aim to create a coordinated system where skin NTDs are identified early, managed appropriately at either facility or household level, and supported through engaged and informed communities.
For achieving objective 2 we implemented a multi-centre Phase 3 randomised controlled trial, which was conducted in three clinical sites in Ghana. The primary outcome measure was the mean time to clearance of viable mycobacteria. Cost and health-related quality-of-life data were collected, and a cost-effectiveness analysis was performed. The clinical sites included Pakro health Centre, Wassa Akropong Municipal Hospital and Ga West Municipal Hospital.

This involved evaluation of integrated strategies for early diagnosis, adherence support and stigma reduction to improve targeted participants in the Atwima Mponua District of the Ashanti Region. It included interacting with policy makers, health workers, patients, Opinion leaders and SHEP coordinators who worked with the Ministry of Education
The Clinical Trial involved participants in Pakro Health Centre, Wassa Akropong Municipal, where participants were recruited.
